claim: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels are involved in numerous physiological functions.
source: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels are involved in numerous physiological functions and various mechanisms finely tune their activity, including the Ca2+ ion itself.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Various mechanisms finely tune voltage-gated Ca2+ channel activity, including the Ca2+ ion itself.
source: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels are involved in numerous physiological functions and various mechanisms finely tune their activity, including the Ca2+ ion itself.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: Ca2+-dependent inactivation of L-type Ca2+ channels is well exemplified.
source: This is well exemplified by the Ca2+-dependent inactivation of L-type Ca2+ channels, whose alteration contributes to the dramatic disease Timothy Syndrome.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about L-type channels.

claim: Alteration of Ca2+-dependent inactivation of L-type Ca2+ channels contributes to Timothy Syndrome.
source: This is well exemplified by the Ca2+-dependent inactivation of L-type Ca2+ channels, whose alteration contributes to the dramatic disease Timothy Syndrome.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about Timothy Syndrome.

claim: A long-held view is that T-type Ca2+ channels are not regulated by intracellular Ca2+.
source: For T-type Ca2+ channels, a long-held view is that they are not regulated by intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical scientific consensus.

claim: A rise in submembrane Ca2+ induces a large decrease in T-type current amplitude.
source: We demonstrate that a rise in submembrane Ca2+ induces a large decrease in T-type current amplitude due to a hyperpolarizing shift in the steady-state inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The decrease in T-type current amplitude is due to a hyperpolarizing shift in the steady-state inactivation.
source: We demonstrate that a rise in submembrane Ca2+ induces a large decrease in T-type current amplitude due to a hyperpolarizing shift in the steady-state inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Activation of most representative Ca2+-permeable ionotropic receptors similarly regulate T-type current properties.
source: Activation of most representative Ca2+-permeable ionotropic receptors similarly regulate T-type current properties.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ca2+ entry exerts a feedback control on T-type channel activity by modulating the channel availability.
source: Altogether, our data clearly establish that Ca2+ entry exerts a feedback control on T-type channel activity, by modulating the channel availability, a mechanism that critically links cellular properties of T-type Ca2+ channels to their physiological roles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The permeant Ca2+ ion acts as an intracellular second messenger in voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.
source: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (VGCCs) are unique among voltage-gated ion channels because the permeant Ca2+ ion also acts as an intracellular second messenger, triggering diverse cellular functions (Berridge et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berridge et al., 2003.

claim: VGCCs are involved in neuronal and cardiac excitability, muscle contraction, neurotransmitter release, hormone secretion and gene expression.
source: VGCCs are therefore involved in neuronal and cardiac excitability as well as in muscle contraction, neurotransmitter release, hormone secretion and gene expression (Berridge et al., 2003; Mangoni and Nargeot, 2008; Catterall, 2011; Simms and Zamponi, 2014; Zamponi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Modulation of VGCC activity plays a pivotal role in the regulation of cardiac and brain activities.
source: Consequently the modulation of VGCC activity plays a pivotal role in the regulation of cardiac and brain activities and this modulation is controlled by a variety of processes, including intracellular Ca2+ itself, which provides an important Ca2+-driven feedback control (Eckert and Chad, 1984; Zühlke et al., 1999; Peterson et al., 1999; Liang et al., 2003; Green et al., 2007; Tsuruta et al., 2009; Oliveria et al., 2012; Hall et al., 2013; Zamponi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Intracellular Ca2+ provides an important Ca2+-driven feedback control of VGCC activity.
source: Consequently the modulation of VGCC activity plays a pivotal role in the regulation of cardiac and brain activities and this modulation is controlled by a variety of processes, including intracellular Ca2+ itself, which provides an important Ca2+-driven feedback control (Eckert and Chad, 1984; Zühlke et al., 1999; Peterson et al., 1999; Liang et al., 2003; Green et al., 2007; Tsuruta et al., 2009; Oliveria et al., 2012; Hall et al., 2013; Zamponi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: VGCCs comprise three distinct subfamilies: L-type/Cav1, N-, P/Q-, R-type/Cav2 and T-type/Cav3 channels.
source: VGCCs comprise three distinct subfamilies classified with respect to their biophysical and pharmacological (type), and molecular (Cav) entities: the L-type / Cav1, the N-, P/Q-, R-type / Cav2 and the T-type / Cav3 channels (Ertel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ertel et al., 2000.

claim: Both Cav1 and Cav2 channels are modulated by intracellular Ca2+.
source: It was well demonstrated that both Cav1 and Cav2 channels are modulated by intracellular Ca2+ (Liang et al., 2003; Dick et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2003 and Dick et al., 2008.

claim: A rise in submembrane Ca2+ concentration induces complex effects on Cav1/L-type VGCCs depending on both the Ca2+ concentration and the duration of the Ca2+ entry.
source: For the Cav1 / L-type VGCCs, this Ca2+ feedback mechanism has been extensively studied in a wide spectrum of biological contexts and a rise in submembrane Ca2+ concentration induces complex effects depending on both the Ca2+ concentration and the duration of the Ca2+ entry (Eckert and Chad, 1984; Zühlke et al., 1999; Peterson et al., 1999; Liang et al., 2003; Green et al., 2007; Tsuruta et al., 2009; Oliveria et al., 2012; Hall et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: At the millisecond time scale, Ca2+ entry via L-type channels induces a Ca2+-dependent inactivation characterized by an acceleration of their inactivation kinetics.
source: At the millisecond time scale, the Ca2+ entry via L-type channels induces a Ca2+-dependent inactivation (CDI) characterized by an acceleration of their inactivation kinetics (Eckert and Chad, 1984; Zühlke et al., 1999; Peterson et al., 1999; Liang et al., 2003; Hall et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: For several seconds to a few minutes of stimulation, the cumulative Ca2+ entry induces a decrease of the L-type current amplitude, which is reversible if stimulation ceases for several minutes.
source: For several seconds to a few minutes of stimulation, the cumulative Ca2+ entry induces a decrease of the L-type current amplitude, which is reversible if stimulation ceases for several minutes (Eckert and Chad, 1984; Oliveria et al., 2007, 2012; Hall et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: For longer period of stimulation, or activation of the ionotropic NMDA receptors, L-type channels are internalized, potentially degraded in lysosomes or recycled to the plasma membrane depending on the amount and the duration of the Ca2+ entry.
source: For longer period of stimulation, or activation of the ionotropic NMDA receptors, L-type channels are internalized, potentially degraded in lysosomes or recycled to the plasma membrane depending on the amount and the duration of the Ca2+ entry (Green et al., 2007; Tsuruta et al., 2009; Hall et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The precise Ca2+-dependent regulation of the L-type channel activity has a strong physiological role in avoiding cytotoxicity arising from Ca2+ overload.
source: This precise Ca2+-dependent regulation of the L-type channel activity has a strong physiological role in avoiding cytotoxicity arising from Ca2+ overload (Lee et al., 1999; Berridge et al., 2003; Green et al., 2007; Tsuruta et al., 2009; Hall et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Alteration of the Ca2+-dependent regulation of the L-type channels is deleterious and has important pathophysiological consequences as observed in the Timothy syndrome.
source: Consequently, alteration of the Ca2+-dependent regulation of the L-type channels is deleterious and has important pathophysiological consequences as observed in the Timothy syndrome (Splawski et al., 2004; Barrett and Tsien, 2008; Blaich et al., 2012; Limpitikul et al., 2014; Dick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: It is presently unknown whether a change in intracellular Ca2+ concentration is involved in regulating T-type Ca2+ channel activity.
source: Contrasting with this well-established Ca2+-dependent regulation of the L-type channels, it is presently unknown whether a change in intracellular Ca2+ concentration is involved in regulating T-type Ca2+ channel activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: T-type/Cav3 channels are specifically activated by small membrane depolarization below the threshold of classical sodium action potentials.
source: The low-voltage-activated, T-type/Cav3 channels are specifically activated by small membrane depolarization below the threshold of classical sodium action potentials, producing a Ca2+ entry near the resting membrane potential and low-threshold Ca2+ spikes (Huguenard, 1996, 1998; Perez-Reyes, 2003; Zamponi, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: T-type/Cav3 channels produce a Ca2+ entry near the resting membrane potential and low-threshold Ca2+ spikes.
source: The low-voltage-activated, T-type/Cav3 channels are specifically activated by small membrane depolarization below the threshold of classical sodium action potentials, producing a Ca2+ entry near the resting membrane potential and low-threshold Ca2+ spikes (Huguenard, 1996, 1998; Perez-Reyes, 2003; Zamponi, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Availability of Cav3 channels is critically regulated by the resting membrane potential to control T-type channel activity.
source: Importantly, availability of Cav3 channels is critically regulated by the resting membrane potential to control T-type channel activity.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Cav3 channels are partially inactivated in the range of the resting membrane potential of most neurons.
source: Because of the negative range of their steady-state inactivation (V0.5 near −70 mV), Cav3 channels are partially inactivated (reduced availability) in the range of the resting membrane potential of most neurons and a membrane hyperpolarization (usually triggered by inhibitory postsynaptic events) is needed to allow their recovery from inactivation (de-inactivation) and their subsequent opening (Huguenard, 1996; Perez-Reyes, 2003; Zamponi, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A membrane hyperpolarization is needed to allow Cav3 channels recovery from inactivation and their subsequent opening.
source: Because of the negative range of their steady-state inactivation (V0.5 near −70 mV), Cav3 channels are partially inactivated (reduced availability) in the range of the resting membrane potential of most neurons and a membrane hyperpolarization (usually triggered by inhibitory postsynaptic events) is needed to allow their recovery from inactivation (de-inactivation) and their subsequent opening (Huguenard, 1996; Perez-Reyes, 2003; Zamponi, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cav3 channels mediate rebound burst firing in many types of neurons, especially in the thalamo-cortical circuit.
source: This behavior is of particular importance in many types of neurons, in which Cav3 channels mediate rebound burst firing, especially in the thalamo-cortical circuit, where Cav3 channels control transition between awake and sleep states (Huguenard, 1996; Perez-Reyes, 2003; Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2009; Zamponi, 2016; Tatsuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cav3 channels control transition between awake and sleep states in the thalamo-cortical circuit.
source: This behavior is of particular importance in many types of neurons, in which Cav3 channels mediate rebound burst firing, especially in the thalamo-cortical circuit, where Cav3 channels control transition between awake and sleep states (Huguenard, 1996; Perez-Reyes, 2003; Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2009; Zamponi, 2016; Tatsuki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cav3 channels are involved in the control of the Ca2+ homeostasis.
source: Overall, Cav3 channels are involved in the control of the Ca2+ homeostasis (Chemin et al., 2000; Bijlenga et al., 2000; Perez-Reyes, 2003), in Ca2+-dependent differentiation of neuronal, muscular and neuroendocrine cells (Bijlenga et al., 2000; Mariot et al., 2002; Chemin et al., 2002b), as well as in Ca2+ overload toxicity in ischemia (Nikonenko et al., 2005; Bancila et al., 2011; Gouriou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cav3 channels are involved in Ca2+-dependent differentiation of neuronal, muscular and neuroendocrine cells.
source: Overall, Cav3 channels are involved in the control of the Ca2+ homeostasis (Chemin et al., 2000; Bijlenga et al., 2000; Perez-Reyes, 2003), in Ca2+-dependent differentiation of neuronal, muscular and neuroendocrine cells (Bijlenga et al., 2000; Mariot et al., 2002; Chemin et al., 2002b), as well as in Ca2+ overload toxicity in ischemia (Nikonenko et al., 2005; Bancila et al., 2011; Gouriou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cav3 channels are involved in Ca2+ overload toxicity in ischemia.
source: Overall, Cav3 channels are involved in the control of the Ca2+ homeostasis (Chemin et al., 2000; Bijlenga et al., 2000; Perez-Reyes, 2003), in Ca2+-dependent differentiation of neuronal, muscular and neuroendocrine cells (Bijlenga et al., 2000; Mariot et al., 2002; Chemin et al., 2002b), as well as in Ca2+ overload toxicity in ischemia (Nikonenko et al., 2005; Bancila et al., 2011; Gouriou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: An increase in the Cav3 channel activity has been implicated in several diseases including epilepsy, chronic pain, autism and primary aldosteronism.
source: Importantly, an increase in the Cav3 channel activity has been implicated in several diseases including epilepsy, chronic pain, autism and primary aldosteronism (Beenhakker and Huguenard, 2009; Zamponi, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is no evidence yet that Cav3 channels are regulated by intracellular Ca2+ ions and/or by Ca2+ entry.
source: Although it is evident that a tight control of Cav3 channel activity is necessary to maintain Ca2+ homeostasis, there is no evidence yet that Cav3 channels are regulated by intracellular Ca2+ ions and/or by Ca2+ entry.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Dynamic changes and localized increase in the intracellular Ca2+ concentration at the vicinity of Cav3 channels control availability of these channels.
source: We provide evidence that dynamic changes and localized increase in the intracellular Ca2+ concentration at the vicinity Cav3 channels control availability of these channels, which underlies this novel regulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: D-hair mechanoreceptor sensory neurons specifically express a high density of T-type channels.
source: In D-hair mechanoreceptor sensory neurons, which specifically express a high density of T-type channels (Shin et al., 2003; Dubreuil et al., 2004; Voisin et al., 2016), extracellular perfusion of 10 µM ionomycin induced a potent decrease of the T-type current (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Extracellular perfusion of 10 µM ionomycin induced a potent decrease of the T-type current in D-hair mechanoreceptor sensory neurons.
source: In D-hair mechanoreceptor sensory neurons, which specifically express a high density of T-type channels (Shin et al., 2003; Dubreuil et al., 2004; Voisin et al., 2016), extracellular perfusion of 10 µM ionomycin induced a potent decrease of the T-type current (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Ionomycin-induced T-type current inhibition in D-hair neurons was approximately 85% on average.
source: This current inhibition (~85% in average) occurred in the minute range (Figure 1b) and was associated with a large hyperpolarizing shift in the steady-state inactivation curve (~22 mV, p<0.001, Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Ionomycin-induced T-type current inhibition in D-hair neurons occurred in the minute range.
source: This current inhibition (~85% in average) occurred in the minute range (Figure 1b) and was associated with a large hyperpolarizing shift in the steady-state inactivation curve (~22 mV, p<0.001, Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Ionomycin-induced T-type current inhibition in D-hair neurons was associated with a large hyperpolarizing shift in the steady-state inactivation curve of approximately 22 mV.
source: This current inhibition (~85% in average) occurred in the minute range (Figure 1b) and was associated with a large hyperpolarizing shift in the steady-state inactivation curve (~22 mV, p<0.001, Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: Ionomycin potently inhibited the Cav3.1, Cav3.2 and Cav3.3 currents by about 80%.
source: Ionomycin potently inhibited the Cav3.1, Cav3.2 and Cav3.3 currents by about 80% (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Ionomycin effect on Cav3 currents was combined with an acceleration of the inactivation kinetics approximately 3 times.
source: This effect was combined with an acceleration of the inactivation kinetics (~3 times, Figure 1e) and a hyperpolarizing shift in the steady-state inactivation curve (~23 mV, p<0.001, Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Ionomycin effect on Cav3 currents was combined with a hyperpolarizing shift in the steady-state inactivation curve of approximately 23 mV.
source: This effect was combined with an acceleration of the inactivation kinetics (~3 times, Figure 1e) and a hyperpolarizing shift in the steady-state inactivation curve (~23 mV, p<0.001, Figure 1f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1f with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: Recombinant Cav3 channels, especially Cav3.3 channels, can generate large entry of Ca2+ during fast stimulation protocols.
source: Considering that recombinant Cav3 channels, especially Cav3.3 channels, can generate large entry of Ca2+ during fast stimulation protocols (Huguenard, 1998; Kozlov et al., 1999; Chemin et al., 2002a; Perez-Reyes, 2003), we have investigated whether these channels might be modulated by their own activity.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Cav3.3 current amplitude recorded using fast TP stimulation (1 Hz) progressively decreased to approximately 50% of the control value.
source: The Cav3.3 current amplitude recorded using fast TP stimulation (1 Hz) progressively decreased to ~50% of the control value (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The Cav3.3 current decrease was maximal and stable after approximately 40 s with an average half-time of 18 s.
source: In average, the current decrease was maximal and stable after ~40 s with an average half-time of 18 s (Figure 2a and f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and 2f.

claim: The Cav3.3 current decrease was associated with a marked acceleration of the inactivation kinetics approximately 3 times after 40 s stimulation.
source: The current decrease was also associated with a marked acceleration of the inactivation kinetics (Figure 2a), ~3 times after 40 s stimulation (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and 2e.

claim: The Cav3.3 current inhibition effect was fully reversible and activity-dependent.
source: This effect was fully reversible and activity-dependent since the stopping of the TP stimulation for only 5 s already induced ~30% recovery of the current.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Stopping of the TP stimulation for only 5 s already induced approximately 30% recovery of the Cav3.3 current.
source: This effect was fully reversible and activity-dependent since the stopping of the TP stimulation for only 5 s already induced ~30% recovery of the current.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Recovery of Cav3.3 current was complete after approximately 2 min without TP stimulation with an average half-time of 20 s.
source: Recovery was complete after ~2 min without TP stimulation with an average half-time of 20 s (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The Cav3.3 current was unchanged when the TP was set at +100 mV.
source: In contrast with the data obtained for a TP at −30 mV (Figure 2a), the Cav3.3 current was unchanged when the TP was set at +100 mV (a membrane potential value above the reversal potential of Cav3 current, leading to an outward current, Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The decrease in current amplitude observed for a fast TP stimulation at −30 mV does not involve a voltage-dependent inactivation process that would occur at high frequency of stimulation.
source: These experiments clearly indicate that the decrease in current amplitude observed for a fast TP stimulation at −30 mV does not involve a voltage-dependent inactivation process that would occur at high frequency of stimulation, but is rather related to the Ca2+ entry via Cav3.3 channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing TP at -30 mV and +100 mV.

claim: The decrease in current amplitude observed for a fast TP stimulation at −30 mV is related to the Ca2+ entry via Cav3.3 channels.
source: These experiments clearly indicate that the decrease in current amplitude observed for a fast TP stimulation at −30 mV does not involve a voltage-dependent inactivation process that would occur at high frequency of stimulation, but is rather related to the Ca2+ entry via Cav3.3 channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing TP at -30 mV and +100 mV.

claim: In the absence of extracellular Ca2+, the sodium inward current through Cav3.3 channels remained unchanged during the time of the fast TP protocol at −30 mV.
source: Also, in the absence of extracellular Ca2+, the sodium inward current through Cav3.3 channels remained unchanged during the time of the fast TP protocol at −30 mV (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: No change in Cav3.3 current properties were obtained in the presence of 2 mM extracellular Ca2+ when cells were dialyzed with an intracellular medium containing BAPTA instead of EGTA.
source: In addition, no change in Cav3.3 current properties were obtained in the presence of 2 mM extracellular Ca2 when cells were dialyzed with an intracellular medium containing BAPTA instead of EGTA (Figure 2d and e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d and 2e.

claim: The difference in susceptibility to BAPTA and EGTA is characteristic of a process driven by a localized rise in submembrane Ca2+, without the need for a global Ca2+ increase.
source: This difference in susceptibility to BAPTA and EGTA is characteristic of a process driven by a localized rise in submembrane Ca2+, without the need for a global Ca2+ increase (Marty and Neher, 1985; Roberts, 1993; Deisseroth et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The application of 1, 10 or 100 µM Ca2+ to the internal side of the membrane in the inside-out patch configuration for more than 60 s did not induce a significant inhibition of the Cav3.3 current.
source: In this configuration, the application of 1, 10 or 100 µM Ca2+ during more than 60 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) did not induce a significant inhibition of the Cav3.3 current as compared to a control solution containing 1 mM EGTA/0 mM Ca2+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that Ca2+-induced Cav3.3 inhibition requires some additional components preserved in the whole-cell configuration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and 1c.

claim: Ca2+-induced Cav3.3 inhibition requires some additional components preserved in the whole-cell configuration.
source: In this configuration, the application of 1, 10 or 100 µM Ca2+ during more than 60 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) did not induce a significant inhibition of the Cav3.3 current as compared to a control solution containing 1 mM EGTA/0 mM Ca2+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that Ca2+-induced Cav3.3 inhibition requires some additional components preserved in the whole-cell configuration.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in inside-out patches.

claim: The decrease in Cav3.3 current gradually developed with the increase in TP frequency.
source: The decrease in Cav3.3 current gradually developed with the increase in TP frequency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No decrease in Cav3.3 current was observed at low frequency of TP (0.033 Hz).
source: While no decrease was observed at low frequency of TP (0.033 Hz), the decrease in Cav3.3 current became significant at 0.2 Hz and further increased at 0.5 and 1 Hz (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The decrease in Cav3.3 current became significant at 0.2 Hz and further increased at 0.5 and 1 Hz.
source: While no decrease was observed at low frequency of TP (0.033 Hz), the decrease in Cav3.3 current became significant at 0.2 Hz and further increased at 0.5 and 1 Hz (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The amplitude of Cav3.1 current decreased modestly and only at the TP frequency of 1 Hz.
source: The amplitude of Cav3.1 current decreased modestly and only at the TP frequency of 1 Hz (Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–b.

claim: The Cav3.2 current showed no inhibition but rather a small increase in amplitude at fast stimulation.
source: Contrasting with the results described above, the Cav3.2 current showed no inhibition but rather a small increase in amplitude at fast stimulation (Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 2d–e).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g and Figure 2—figure supplement 2d–e.

claim: For Cav3.1 channels, the decrease in current amplitude was associated with faster inactivation kinetics.
source: For Cav3.1 channels, the decrease in current amplitude was associated with faster inactivation kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), while inactivation kinetics of the Cav3.2 current was unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Inactivation kinetics of the Cav3.2 current was unchanged during fast stimulation.
source: For Cav3.1 channels, the decrease in current amplitude was associated with faster inactivation kinetics (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), while inactivation kinetics of the Cav3.2 current was unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2f.

claim: Cav3.1 current amplitude and inactivation kinetics were unchanged after dialyzing the cells with BAPTA.
source: Similar to that described for the Cav3.3 current, Cav3.1 current amplitude and inactivation kinetics were unchanged after dialyzing the cells with BAPTA (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The recovery kinetics of the Cav3.3 current was unaffected at the three inter-pulse durations tested (100, 400 or 1000 ms).
source: These experiments revealed that the recovery kinetics of the Cav3.3 current was unaffected at the three inter-pulse durations tested (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The steady-state inactivation of Cav3.3 current was strongly modified using fast stimulation protocols.
source: In contrast, we found that the steady-state inactivation of Cav3.3 current was strongly modified using fast stimulation protocols.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fast stimulation protocol produced a approximately 10 mV hyperpolarizing shift in the V0.5 value of the steady-state inactivation curve of Cav3.3 (from −72.4 mV for Stim 1 to −81.1 mV for the Stim 40, p<0.001).
source: This fast stimulation protocol produced a ~10 mV hyperpolarizing shift in the V0.5 value of the steady-state inactivation curve (from −72.4 mV for Stim 1 to −81.1 mV for the Stim 40, p<0.001), without any change in the slope of the inactivation curve (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: Fast stimulation protocol produced no change in the slope of the inactivation curve of Cav3.3.
source: This fast stimulation protocol produced a ~10 mV hyperpolarizing shift in the V0.5 value of the steady-state inactivation curve (from −72.4 mV for Stim 1 to −81.1 mV for the Stim 40, p<0.001), without any change in the slope of the inactivation curve (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The hyperpolarizing shift in steady-state inactivation effect was lost in the presence of intracellular BAPTA.
source: Importantly, this effect was lost in the presence of intracellular BAPTA (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Fast stimulation of Cav3.3 current induced a small but significant leftward shift in the steady-state activation (from −52.6 to −55.9 mV, p<0.01).
source: In addition, we found that the fast stimulation of Cav3.3 current also induced a small but significant leftward shift in the steady-state activation (from −52.6 to −55.9 mV, p<0.01) as well as an increase in the slope of the activation curve (from 4.7 to 5.6 mV, p<0.05, Figure 3e–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e–f with statistical significance p<0.01.

claim: Fast stimulation of Cav3.3 current induced an increase in the slope of the activation curve (from 4.7 to 5.6 mV, p<0.05).
source: In addition, we found that the fast stimulation of Cav3.3 current also induced a small but significant leftward shift in the steady-state activation (from −52.6 to −55.9 mV, p<0.01) as well as an increase in the slope of the activation curve (from 4.7 to 5.6 mV, p<0.05, Figure 3e–f).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e–f with statistical significance p<0.05.

claim: Paired-pulse protocols revealed a approximately 5 mV hyperpolarizing shift of the steady-state inactivation curve for Cav3.1 channels (p<0.001).
source: Similar findings were obtained with Cav3.1 channels since these paired-pulse protocols revealed a ~5 mV hyperpolarizing shift of the steady-state inactivation curve (p<0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b) with no significant effect on the recovery kinetics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) and the steady-state activation curve of the Cav3.1 current (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b with statistical significance p<0.001.

claim: Paired-pulse protocols had no significant effect on the recovery kinetics of Cav3.1 current.
source: Similar findings were obtained with Cav3.1 channels since these paired-pulse protocols revealed a ~5 mV hyperpolarizing shift of the steady-state inactivation curve (p<0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b) with no significant effect on the recovery kinetics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) and the steady-state activation curve of the Cav3.1 current (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Paired-pulse protocols had no significant effect on the steady-state activation curve of the Cav3.1 current.
source: Similar findings were obtained with Cav3.1 channels since these paired-pulse protocols revealed a ~5 mV hyperpolarizing shift of the steady-state inactivation curve (p<0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–b) with no significant effect on the recovery kinetics (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) and the steady-state activation curve of the Cav3.1 current (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The model indicated that the Cav3.3 current elicited from HP −70 mV would decrease approximately 75% according to the shift in the steady-state inactivation.
